Network Infiltration Dynamics · Simulation Report

Detectability Collapse

A concentrated asymmetry injected into a bound network is not concealed by the intruder. It is concealed by the medium, which equalizes the very contrast that detection depends on. Five parameter sweeps measure how fast, and at what cost to the origin.

Abstract

Network Infiltration Dynamics treats infiltration as a single event observed from two ends: a concentrated asymmetry is injected across a network's aperture, and the network's own mechanisms flatten it until the intruder becomes a property of the cluster. The governing inversion is that flattening, which destroys an ordinary signal's leverage, completes a pathogen's installation — because detection requires contrast, and equalization destroys contrast.

This report interprets five parameter sweeps and two result tables produced by an agent-based implementation of that theory. Across 23 runs on a 120-node Watts–Strogatz network, three findings hold. First, detectability collapse is governed principally by cond, the per-path transmissivity of the medium, which sets the time scale; ports and noise saturate after roughly four ports and 0.5 noise respectively. Second, installation and concealment are separate events with a measurable gap: the intruder is a majority property of the field for 0.82 to 1.68 seconds before contrast falls below the detection threshold. Third, the fastest-installing configuration deliberately lowers clustering to 0.39, contradicting the theoretical expectation and isolating a real distinction between conduction speed and containment.

§1Theoretical framework

The simulation operationalizes six topics drawn from the source corpus. Four of them (1–4) are one continuous mechanism — the Conductive Pathogen decomposed — while topic 5 describes infiltration by density and topic 6 infiltration by disruption. Each topic is represented in the model by exactly one tunable parameter, which is what makes the sweeps interpretable as tests of the theory rather than as arbitrary parameter scans.

The central claim is directional. Entry requires potential difference: standing above baseline is simultaneously the property that admits the intruder and the property that makes it dangerous. Establishment then requires the opposite — the erasure of that same difference. An infiltration that never equalizes stays visible; one that equalizes fully cannot be read as anomalous, because no baseline survives to read it against.

§2Model and methods

2.1Topology

The substrate is a Watts–Strogatz ring lattice of N = 120 nodes with degree K = 4. The clustering parameter enters inversely, as the rewiring probability p_rewire = 1 − clust. High clustering therefore produces a near-pure ring lattice with long characteristic path lengths; low clustering produces abundant long-range shortcuts. This inversion matters for interpreting Figure 3 and is taken up in §4.4.

Each node i carries a concentration cᵢ ∈ [0,1], an adoption ceiling, a fixed structural density dᵢ ~ U(0.32, 1.00), and a convergence state γᵢ.

2.2Transmission rule

An uninfected node evaluates every neighbour that is infected and above the carrier threshold cₖ ≥ 0.28. Each such neighbour supplies an independent conductive path, and the paths compound multiplicatively — the direct implementation of topic 2.

Adoption probability
pᵢₖ = clamp( cond · grad · (cₖ − cᵢ) · σᵢ , 0 , 0.96 )
p_adopt(i) = 1 − ∏ₖ (1 − pᵢₖ)
σᵢ = (1 + cap(1 + cap − dᵢ)·0.35) · (1 + (1 − γᵢ)·2.2)
γᵢ → 1 − noise · (0.35 + 0.65·uᵢ), uᵢ ~ U(0,1)

The term (cₖ − cᵢ) is the potential difference across a single path: transmission is driven by the gap, not by the neighbour's absolute state. The susceptibility factor σᵢ carries topics 5 and 6 — thinner nodes are absorbed faster, and destabilized nodes adopt up to 3.2× more readily. Adoption is drawn each step with probability p_adopt · dt · 3.4.

An adopting node inherits a diluted ceiling, ceilᵢ = max(0.55, 0.986 · maxₖ ceilₖ). The signal loses 1.4% of its concentration per replication hop and cannot fall below 0.55. This is why the field's mean asymptotes near 97% rather than 100%, visible in Figure 5.

2.3Observables

Four metrics are recorded each step. The distinction between them is the analytical core of this report, because they do not move together.

Metric definitions
Baseline B(t) = (1/N) ∑ᵢ cᵢ
Carriers F(t) = |{ i : infected }| / N
Detectability D(t) = maxᵢ cᵢ − B(t)
Traceability T(t) = clamp( (1 − 0.16(ports−1)) · (1 − 0.82·F) , 0 , 1 )

Detectability is a contrast, not an amount. It measures the gap between the hottest node and the field mean. It is therefore maximal at injection, when one node sits at 1.0 against a field of 0, and collapses toward zero when the field has risen to meet the intruder — not because the intruder weakened, but because the reference against which it was anomalous no longer exists.

2.4Run protocol and event definitions

  • Installation (t_install) is declared the first time carrier fraction exceeds F > 0.92. It is a coverage event.
  • Concealment (t_det≤5%) is the first time detectability falls to or below 5%. It is a contrast event, and is recorded as undefined when a run's residual contrast never reaches that threshold.
  • Ports are placed by greedy maximal spacing across the layout, approximating independent entry points rather than adjacent ones.
  • Every figure reports a single stochastic run per parameter value. No averaging over seeds was performed; see §5.

§2.5The model, running

Everything specified above is embedded below: the same index.html implementation whose sweeps produced every figure in §3, running live in this page. The transmission rule of §2.2 is its step function, and the four readouts under the frame are the observables of §2.3 measured on the run in progress.

The configurations of Table 3 are wired to the buttons above the frame, and each figure in §3 carries a control that loads the parameter set that figure reports and injects. Expand lifts the model to the full window, where the field has enough width for the control rail to sit beside it; the run is not restarted when it expands or closes.

§3Results

Five sweeps, presented in the order of the mechanism: entry multiplicity, medium transmissivity, target destabilization, whole-regime comparison, and finally the decomposition of a single optimized run into its four constituent metrics.

3.1Multi-port injection and origin dissolution

Figure 1 sweeps the number of simultaneous injection points from one to eight, holding the medium at default. The family of curves separates cleanly at low port counts and then converges: the gap between one and three ports is larger than the gap between five and eight combined.

What the sweep shows

Parallelized spend is real but bounded. Installation time falls from 5.10 s at one port to a minimum of 3.17 s at six — a 38% reduction — and then rises again at seven and eight ports. The theory's prediction that the network is crossed in roughly the time to cross one cluster is confirmed in direction, but the benefit is exhausted well before the parameter's range is. Beyond about four ports the field is already being saturated from enough directions that additional entry points contend for the same uninfected nodes rather than opening new frontiers.

The floor drops with port count. Final detectability falls monotonically from 5.5% to 3.2%. The mechanism is worth stating precisely: detectability is max cᵢ − B, and the maximum is always a port node held at c = 1. Adding ports adds more nodes pinned at the ceiling, which raises the mean without raising the maximum. The residual scar shrinks because the field's average rises closer to the intruder's peak.

One and two ports never conceal. Both runs install — they reach 92% carriers — but their residual contrast settles at 5.5% and 5.1%, above the threshold, so t_det≤5% is undefined. This is the sharpest operational result in the table: installation does not imply concealment. A single-port infiltration can fully saturate a network and still leave a permanent, readable anomaly at its entry point.

Finding · Origin dissolution

Traceability falls by a constant 2.88 percentage points per added port — 18.0, 15.1, 12.2, 9.4, 6.5, 3.6, 0.7 — and clamps to exactly zero at eight ports. The linearity is exact because it is definitional: the model's traceability term contains the factor (1 − 0.16(ports−1)), which vanishes at ports = 7.25.

This is an assumption of the model, not a discovery from it. Origin dissolution is encoded rather than emergent, and the sweep should be read as illustrating the theory's claim rather than as evidence for it. The one genuinely emergent contribution is the second factor, (1 − 0.82·F): traceability also decays as coverage grows, so even single-port entry falls to 18% once the field is saturated.

3.2Conductance sets the time scale

Figure 2 sweeps per-path transmissivity from 0.06 to 0.40. Unlike the port sweep, this family shows no saturation across its range and no crossing of curves — the ordering is strict, and the spacing widens toward the low end.

Conductance is the dominant time-scaling parameter. It enters the adoption probability as a direct linear multiplier on every path simultaneously, before the multiplicative combination across neighbours. Doubling conductance does not double one path's chance; it raises every path's chance, and the compounding does the rest. This is why the sweep produces the widest dynamic range of any single parameter in the study.

The low end changes the shape, not just the speed. Curves at cond ≥ 0.18 are sigmoid: a shoulder, a steep collapse, a floor. The cond = 0.06 curve is qualitatively different — it descends nearly linearly, spends roughly four seconds drifting between 15% and 5%, and never develops a clean floor within the window. In theoretical terms, this is a medium that cannot equalize faster than an observer could integrate. The asymmetry persists long enough to be read.

Finding · The defensive parameter

Of the parameters swept, conductance is the one whose reduction most reliably prevents establishment. Ports and noise both saturate; conductance does not. A medium that lowers per-path transmissivity does not merely delay the intruder — it holds the contrast above the detection threshold long enough for the anomaly to remain an anomaly.

3.3Convergence denial accelerates but does not conceal

Figure 4 sweeps convergence-denial noise from 0.00 to 0.70. This is topic 6 — infiltration by disruption — entering the model through the susceptibility term: destabilized nodes, unable to settle, adopt the incoming signal more readily.

The effect is real but compressed. Full-range noise buys roughly 2.4 seconds — about a 35% reduction in time to concealment — against conductance's threefold. More telling is where the gains stop. The susceptibility multiplier grows linearly with noise, from about 1.22 at the default 0.15 to about 2.04 at 0.70, yet the timing curves converge after 0.50. The reason is structural: per-path adoption probability is clamped at 0.96 and paths compound multiplicatively, so once a node has two or three hot neighbours its combined probability is already close to 1. Additional susceptibility has nothing left to buy.

Noise changes when, not whether. Every curve in Figure 4 lands on the same residual floor. Destabilizing the target population does not lower the permanent contrast the infiltration leaves behind; it only shortens the interval before that floor is reached. Under this model, convergence denial is an accelerant on the transmission side and contributes nothing to concealment.

The parameters compose multiplicatively, and so do their opposites. The Optimized regime improves five parameters at once and installs 3.7× faster than default while reaching concealment 2.8× faster. The Slow regime worsens the same parameters and does not merely take longer — it fails to install at all. Weak gradient, minimal conductance, a single port, and high clustering compound into a medium that cannot equalize the injected asymmetry within any reasonable observation window. The intruder is present, spreading, and continuously visible.

Different routes reach the same speed. The High-noise regime runs a substantially weaker gradient (1.50 against 1.97) and conductance (0.220 against 0.315) than Optimized, yet installs in 1.40 s against 1.10 s and conceals in 2.25 s against 1.92 s — within about 25%. It compensates with the highest noise in the study (0.65) and seven ports. Target destabilization and entry multiplicity substitute for raw medium transmissivity. There is no single privileged route to installation.

3.5Trajectory decomposition

Figure 5 unpacks the Optimized run into its four observables. This is the figure that makes the theory's central inversion legible, because it plots the intruder's spread and the field's rise on the same axis.

Reading the crossing

The decisive moment is at approximately t = 0.5 s, where the falling detectability curve crosses the rising baseline curve near 50%. Before it, the intruder is a spike against a flat field. After it, the field's mean has risen past the intruder's remaining contrast. Nothing happened to the intruder at that point — its concentration is unchanged and its ceiling is fixed. What changed is the reference. This is topic 1 rendered as a single graphical event: the medium's equalization, not the intruder's behaviour, is what performs the concealment.

Note also that baseline lags carriers throughout and asymptotes near 97% rather than 100%. Carrier fraction counts nodes that have adopted; baseline measures how much they carry. The gap is the 1.4% per-hop dilution: nodes further from a port settle at lower ceilings, so a fully saturated network still holds slightly less signal than its ports do. That residual gap is precisely the 3% detectability floor at which the run terminates.

Finding · The exposure window

Installation occurs at 1.10 s, but detectability is still near 29% at that moment and does not fall below 5% until 1.92 s. For 0.82 seconds the intruder is a majority property of the network and remains measurably anomalous. This interval appears in every completed run in the study: 1.33 s at default, 0.97 to 1.68 s across the port sweep, 0.85 s in the High-noise regime.

The window narrows under aggressive configurations but never closes. Across the runs where both events are defined, the mean is roughly 1.2 s and the minimum is 0.82 s. Under this model there is no tested setting at which installation and concealment coincide — coverage always precedes contrast collapse.

§4Discussion

4.1Two events, not one

The theory describes infiltration as one event seen from two ends. The simulation's most useful contribution is to show that under measurement those two ends separate in time. Installation is a coverage property of the intruder; concealment is a contrast property of the field. They are produced by the same process at different rates, and the lag between them is the interval in which an infiltration is both established and detectable.

Every parameter that accelerates installation also narrows this window, but none eliminates it, because the two events are driven by different quantities: F saturates when the last node adopts, while D continues falling as slower nodes relax toward their ceilings after adoption. The metric that closes last is always the one that measures contrast.

4.2Saturation is the general shape

Three of the four swept parameters saturate, and they do so for the same structural reason. Because parallel paths compound as 1 − ∏(1 − pᵢₖ) with each term clamped at 0.96, combined adoption probability approaches 1 once a node has a small number of infected neighbours. Every parameter that raises per-path probability — ports by adding frontiers, noise by raising susceptibility, gradient by widening the gap — runs into the same ceiling. Conductance is the exception only in degree: it multiplies every path at once, so it reaches the ceiling later.

The practical reading is that infiltration effort has sharply diminishing returns past a modest threshold. Six ports is not meaningfully worse than eight; noise at 0.50 is not meaningfully worse than 0.70. The marginal investment that continues to pay is in the medium's conductance — which is generally the parameter an intruder controls least.

4.3The residual scar

No run reaches zero detectability. The floor ranges from 3.2% to 5.5%, and it is set by the interaction of two model features: ports are permanently pinned at c = 1, and adopting nodes inherit ceilings diluted 1.4% per hop. The maximum therefore never falls, while the mean never quite rises to meet it.

This is theoretically consequential. The corpus claims that equalization destroys contrast and therefore destroys detectability. The simulation qualifies that: equalization destroys most contrast, asymptotically, and what survives is located exactly at the entry points. An observer with sufficient resolution and a stable reference could in principle still find the ports — which is why the 5% threshold, and not zero, is the operative definition of concealment throughout this study.

4.4Clustering: speed against containment

The most interesting disagreement between theory and simulation is topic 4. The corpus holds that high clustering yields speed, pattern-persistence, and invisibility from one cause. The Optimized regime instead sets clustering to 0.39 — well below default — while the Slow regime sets it to 0.85.

The disagreement is a matter of scope, and resolving it sharpens both claims. In this implementation clustering enters inversely as rewiring probability, so high clustering yields a near-ring lattice: fast local conduction, but long global path lengths. Low clustering yields small-world shortcuts and fast global saturation. The simulation measures whole-field equalization, which shortcuts dominate. The theory's claim concerns what happens within a bound cluster, and what fails to radiate out of it.

Both are consistent if clustering is understood as a containment parameter rather than a velocity parameter. High clustering makes an infiltration fast and unobservable inside its cluster, and slow to cross the network. Low clustering makes it fast across the network and correspondingly more exposed in transit. The model contains no external observer node, so it can measure the velocity face of this trade and not the observability face. Topic 4 is therefore only half tested.

§5Limitations

  • Single-seed runs. Each curve is one stochastic realization. The non-monotonic installation times in Table 2 — 3.17 s at six ports rising to 3.68 s at eight — are within plausible run-to-run variance and should not be read as a real reversal. Confidence intervals would require repeated seeds, which were not run.
  • Origin dissolution is encoded, not emergent. Traceability is computed from a closed-form expression in ports and F rather than by simulating an actual back-tracing procedure. Its exact linearity in Table 2 is an artifact of that formula. Topic 3's origin-dissolution claim is illustrated by the model, not tested by it.
  • Topic 5 is untested. Capacity differential (cap) is implemented in the susceptibility term but held at 1.20 in all 23 runs. The Sovereignty Trade — absorption sought by the absorbed party — has no sweep and no result in this study.
  • No observer, therefore no true detection model. Detectability is defined as a global statistic, max c − mean c, computed with full knowledge of every node. A real detector has partial visibility and a noise threshold of its own. This is also why topic 4's invisibility claim cannot be evaluated here.
  • Approximate read-offs. Figures 2 and 4 have no accompanying source table. Times to threshold quoted for those sweeps are estimated from the plotted curves and carry roughly ±0.2 s of reading error. Note also that Figure 4's noise = 0.15 curve reaches threshold near 5.9 s while Table 3's default run records 5.45 s — separate realizations of nominally identical settings, which itself indicates the scale of seed variance.
  • Fixed scale. All runs use N = 120, K = 4. Whether the saturation thresholds reported in §4.2 hold at other network sizes or degrees is unknown.

§6Conclusion

The simulation supports the framework's central inversion. Across every completed run, detectability falls not because the injected signal weakens but because the field rises to meet it, and Figure 5 locates that reversal at a single crossing point. Flattening completes the installation.

Three results qualify or extend the theory. Installation and concealment are separable events with a floor of roughly 0.8 seconds between them, so an established infiltration passes through a window in which it is both dominant and readable. Effort saturates: ports past four and noise past 0.5 buy almost nothing, while conductance — a property of the medium rather than of the intruder — scales without limit across the tested range and is the parameter whose reduction most reliably prevents establishment. And equalization is asymptotic rather than complete, leaving a 3–5% permanent contrast located precisely at the entry points.

The framework's remaining claims are not yet tested. Origin dissolution is assumed by the traceability formula rather than derived from the dynamics; the capacity differential of topic 5 is implemented but never varied; and the invisibility of a leakless cluster cannot be measured by a model that contains no observer. A model with an explicit partial-visibility detector, and a sweep over cap, would address all three.
